channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Dual benefit of esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia on postoperative pain and mental health outcomes in patients undergoing bariatric surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated whether esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) improves postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes in morbidly obese patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, compared to conventional opioid-based anesthesia.
FINDINGS: 84 patients were randomized (1:1) to esketamine-based OFA (n=42) or opioid-based anesthesia with remifentanil (n=42). 74 (88.1%) completed 3-month follow-up. Postoperative pain intensity within 24 hours was significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.01), with fewer patients experiencing moderate-to-severe pain (P < 0.05). At 3 months, mental health outcomes were significantly better in the esketamine group. Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Pharmacokinetic analysis confirmed rapid esketamine metabolism to active (S)-norketamine.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests esketamine-based OFA may offer dual benefits for acute pain and longer-term mental health without increasing adverse events. Strengths include the double-blind RCT design, clear co-primary outcomes, and pharmacokinetic confirmation. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is limited to 3 months, and the mental health assessment tools are not specified. The lack of blinding details for outcome assessors and potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., baseline mental health severity) limit certainty. The clinical significance of the observed mental health improvement remains uncertain given the short follow-up and unspecified measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine-based OFA may be a promising alternative to opioid-based anesthesia in bariatric surgery, potentially improving immediate postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes. However, larger trials with longer follow-up and validated mental health measures are needed before recommending a change in practice.

item.title: Impact of clozapine on the proteome: A systematic review and functional analyses.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), but its use is limited by serious adverse effects. This systematic review and functional proteomic analysis aimed to integrate proteomic findings associated with clozapine exposure across animal, human, and cell-based models to better understand its mechanisms and potential biomarkers.
FINDINGS: Across 1070 unique proteins altered by clozapine (603 increased, 394 decreased, 73 discordant), 152 were identified in ≥2 studies, with 79 showing concordant directionality. Nine proteins were replicated in ≥3 studies. STRING pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in immune/inflammatory, cellular-stress, and neuronal pathways, with stratified analyses supporting these and related metabolic processes. IPA highlighted necrosis-related processes and downstream effects in cardiovascular, hepatic, and renal systems. No direct comparison of brain and peripheral blood changes was available.
INTERPRETATION: This systematic review provides preliminary evidence that clozapine may influence immune, inflammatory, and cell-death pathways, potentially contributing to adverse effects. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, with limited replication of specific proteins and no direct clinical correlation to treatment response or adverse outcomes. The lack of longitudinal human data and time-series comparisons limits causal inference. The findings are hypothesis-generating and underscore the need for prospective proteomic studies during clozapine initiation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current proteomic data do not yet translate to clinical practice but suggest potential biomarkers for monitoring clozapine-related adverse effects. Clinicians should remain vigilant for immune-mediated complications (e.g., myocarditis) but should not alter prescribing based on these findings alone. Further research is needed to validate these pathways as therapeutic targets or biomarkers.

item.title: Extended-Release Guanfacine Hydrochloride is Safe and Effective as Mono- and Adjunctive Therapy in Children and Adolescents with ADHD: A Naturalistic, Multi-Center, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures-Based Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This naturalistic, multicenter, retrospective cohort study in Türkiye assessed the safety and effectiveness of extended-release guanfacine hydrochloride (GXR) as mono- or adjunctive therapy in 567 children and adolescents (mean age 11.2 years) with ADHD, including high rates of comorbidity (82.4%). The study used clinician-rated CGI scales and parent-reported symptom scales over a 6-month follow-up.
FINDINGS: GXR (median dose 2.0–3.0 mg/day) was associated with symptom improvement, with a low rate of adverse effects. Greater improvement was observed in hyperactive-impulsive (HI) symptoms than inattentive (IA) symptoms. Children with comorbid autism spectrum disorder (ASD; 30% of sample) also showed notable clinical improvement. Baseline symptom severity modified treatment response.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s naturalistic design and lack of a comparator group limit causal inference. The large sample size and real-world setting enhance external validity, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., concurrent therapies, clinician bias) may influence results. The differential effect on HI symptoms and effectiveness in ASD are hypothesis-generating but require confirmation in controlled trials. The low adverse effect rate aligns with prior safety data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GXR may be a reasonable option for ADHD in youth with comorbidities, particularly for hyperactivity-impulsivity or ASD, but clinicians should weigh its modest differential effects against alternatives. Further randomized evidence is needed to guide treatment selection.

item.title: Harm reduction among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO-registered) examined harm reduction policies and services for substance use among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon, a setting with high refugee density and complex legal/healthcare barriers. The review aimed to map service availability, access barriers, and policy gaps to guide interventions.
FINDINGS: Out of 387 records, 29 documents (17 peer-reviewed studies and 12 grey literature reports) were included. No structured harm reduction policies specifically for refugees were identified. Key barriers included legal restrictions, stigma, and poor integration of harm reduction into routine care. Only 4 of 12 grey literature sources mentioned harm reduction provision, and none outlined a comprehensive strategy. Many studies were broad and lacked focused substance-use data in refugee populations.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak and fragmented, with high risk of selection and reporting biases due to reliance on grey literature and heterogeneous, often non-refugee-specific studies. The Joanna Briggs Institute tool was used for risk-of-bias assessment, but the overall quality of included evidence appears low. The lack of policy specificity and integrated services is clear, but causal pathways and effect sizes remain unquantified. Further targeted research is essential to inform policy adaptation and service design.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current harm reduction services in Lebanon do not adequately address refugee needs; clinicians should anticipate gaps in access and advocate for mobile clinics and integrated HCV screening. However, evidence to guide specific clinical interventions is currently insufficient.

item.title: Brain functional changes of suicidal ideation and behaviours: a meta-analysis of task-based fMRI studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pre-registered meta-analysis of 22 task-based fMRI studies examined brain functional changes associated with suicidal ideation and behaviours, comparing 459 suicidal individuals with 681 non-suicidal psychiatric controls. The study aimed to clarify neural underpinnings of suicidality amid methodological heterogeneity.
FINDINGS: In emotion tasks, general suicidality and suicidal behaviours were linked to hyperactivity in the left sensorimotor cortices and hippocampus/parahippocampus, alongside hypoactivity in bilateral visual cortices. Only the visual cortex hypoactivity was consistently replicated across all subgroup analyses. In non-emotion tasks, hyperactivity in the left precentral gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus was observed for general suicidality and suicidal behaviours, consistently replicated across subgroups. Meta-regression showed larger functional changes in frontotemporal regions with higher female proportions and in hippocampal/temporal regions with older participants.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength due to methodological heterogeneity across studies (e.g., varied diagnoses, task types). The consistent finding of visual cortex hypoactivity in emotion tasks and motor/temporal hyperactivity in non-emotion tasks suggests potential neural targets for intervention. However, the clinical significance of these neural changes remains uncertain, as effect sizes and direct clinical outcomes were not reported. The study’s reliance on task-based fMRI and subgroup analyses limits generalisability to routine psychiatric care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings highlight potential neural correlates of suicidality but do not yet translate into actionable clinical tools. Further research is needed to determine if these neural patterns can guide treatment or risk assessment in psychiatric practice.

item.title: Targeting affective cognition during pregnancy to prevent postpartum depression: a randomized controlled trial with parity-specific effects.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested whether prenatal affective cognitive training (PACT) reduces postpartum depression (PPD) risk in pregnant women at heightened risk by targeting negative cognitive biases related to infant cues. The study included 147 pregnant women identified as high-risk, randomized to PACT or care as usual (CAU), with outcomes assessed up to six months postpartum.
FINDINGS: The primary outcome, PPD incidence within six months postpartum, did not differ significantly between PACT (14%) and CAU (24%) overall (p = 0.18). Secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms over the first six weeks postpartum, also showed no significant difference (p = 0.31). However, PACT significantly improved positive interpretation of infant emotions post-intervention (p = 0.003). Exploratory analyses revealed a markedly lower PPD incidence in multiparous women receiving PACT (5%) compared to CAU (35%), with an odds ratio of 0.10 (95% CI [0.01-0.92], p = 0.04). Follow-up data were available for 83% of participants.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is strengthened by its RCT design and structured intervention, but the lack of overall effect on PPD incidence limits conclusions. The significant improvement in affective cognition suggests the intervention may target relevant mechanisms, though clinical significance is unclear. The exploratory parity-specific findings are intriguing but require cautious interpretation due to small subgroup sizes and lack of correction for multiple testing. The high dropout-adjusted follow-up rate (83%) is a strength, but the study’s power may have been insufficient for subgroup analyses. External validity is limited by the selective high-risk population and single-center setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PACT does not currently reduce PPD risk overall, so it cannot be recommended for routine practice. However, the parity-specific effect in multiparous women warrants further investigation in larger, adequately powered trials to determine if targeted interventions could benefit specific subgroups. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting exploratory findings.

item.title: Structure based discovery of antipsychotic-like TAAR1 agonists.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study used computational docking and experimental screening to discover novel trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) agonists as potential antipsychotic agents in schizophrenia, where current dopamine/serotonin-targeting treatments have limited efficacy and side effects.
FINDINGS: From 65 million computationally screened molecules, 55 were experimentally tested, yielding 14 TAAR1 agonists with mid-nanomolar to micromolar potencies. Hit optimization produced nanomolar agonists, with three compounds demonstrating high brain exposure and potency comparable to or exceeding the investigational drug ulotaront. All three normalized amphetamine-induced pre-pulse inhibition in mice (a schizophrenia model) without inducing catalepsy, a common side effect of traditional antipsychotics.
INTERPRETATION: This is a high-throughput, computational-experimental drug discovery study with strong internal validity in its methodology (docking, cryo-EM confirmation, behavioral assays). However, it is entirely preclinical, conducted in mice, and lacks human data. The functional selectivity and lack of catalepsy are promising, but clinical relevance remains uncertain until safety and efficacy are tested in humans. The risk of over-optimization for initial hit rates is noted but not quantified.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change to clinical practice is warranted. These findings justify further development and human trials but should not alter current antipsychotic prescribing.

item.title: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=196) tested whether a single subanesthetic dose of esketamine (0.2 mg/kg IV) reduces postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) on day 3 after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia in women.
FINDINGS: In intention-to-treat analysis, PSD incidence on POD 3 was 13.06% with esketamine vs 24.90% with placebo (risk difference −11.84 pp [95% CI −22.98 to −0.69]; RR 0.52 [95% CI 0.28–0.99]; P=0.047). Per-protocol results were similar. PSD on POD 1 did not differ. Postoperative pain at 30 min was lower with esketamine (P<0.001), but dreaming was more frequent (21.4% vs 11.2%; P=0.048) and recovery metrics were modestly longer (time to alertness 12 vs 11 min; PACU stay 34 vs 31 min; both P≤0.005).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest reduction in PSD at POD 3 with esketamine, but the effect size is small (RR ~0.5) and the confidence interval barely excludes the null. The trial is single-center, short-term, and lacks long-term sleep or functional outcomes. Recovery time and dreaming frequency are slightly increased. Overall certainty is low; confirmation in larger, multicenter studies with longer follow-up is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, esketamine cannot be recommended routinely to prevent PSD after oocyte retrieval; any benefit appears small and may be offset by longer recovery. Monitor for transient side effects and counsel patients accordingly.

item.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence on whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy improves outcomes in major depressive disorder (MDD), and under what conditions such benefits occur.
FINDINGS: The review reports that combined rTMS plus pharmacotherapy may accelerate early symptom improvement, increase response and remission rates, and reduce relapse risk compared with either modality alone. These effects are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains. Neuroimaging studies suggest treatment-associated changes in hippocampal volume and network connectivity, but causal links to clinical improvement remain unclear. Expectancy effects and limitations in sham blinding complicate interpretation of clinical benefits.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes diverse evidence rather than providing pooled effect sizes or definitive conclusions. Strengths include integration across mechanistic and clinical domains; limitations include lack of quantitative meta-analysis, potential selection and publication bias, and unresolved causal pathways. The clinical significance of any observed benefits remains uncertain without standardized effect estimates and rigorous RCT data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of combined rTMS and antidepressants outside research or highly specialized settings. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting heterogeneous findings and await more definitive trials before changing practice.

item.title: Health risks of alcohol consumption in Aotearoa New Zealand: modelling to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This modelling study estimated alcohol-attributable mortality in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ) to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines (LRDGs), using a multi-state life-table model with NZ-specific data and WHO/GBD relative risk (RR) libraries. The cohort consisted of 12-year-olds followed over their lifetime with fixed 2018 exposure and disease rates.
FINDINGS: Males reached a 1-in-100 risk of alcohol-attributable death at 8.6 standard drinks (10 g ethanol) per week [95% UI 3.1–12.0], while females reached this threshold at 9.2 standard drinks [95% UI 3.7–12.4] using WHO RR data. Removing GBD one-star evidence conditions reduced thresholds to 2.7 (males) and 3.5 (females) standard drinks per week. Māori reached risk thresholds at lower consumption levels than non-Māori.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights that current NZ LRDGs may underestimate alcohol-related harm, particularly when excluding low-certainty evidence. Strengths include the use of a validated life-table model and NZ-specific data; limitations include reliance on modelled RRs, fixed 2018 rates, and uncertainty intervals spanning large ranges. The clinical significance is uncertain until guideline committees formally review these thresholds and consider population-specific risks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current NZ low-risk guidelines may need revision, especially for Māori. Clinicians should continue to advise patients on alcohol-related risks while awaiting updated national guidance.

item.title: Clozapine, suicide prevention and risk perception in psychiatry.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This editorial discusses clozapine’s role in reducing suicide risk in treatment-resistant schizophrenia, while noting its underutilization despite evidence of benefit. It explores whether historical risk perception biases in psychiatry contribute to this paradox.
FINDINGS: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with consistent evidence for reducing suicidal behavior, including suicide attempts and completed suicides, in schizophrenia. However, its use is limited by concerns over agranulocytosis and other adverse effects, despite improved monitoring protocols.
INTERPRETATION: As an editorial, this is not a primary research study but a conceptual analysis. It highlights a potential bias in risk assessment—overemphasizing treatment-related mortality (e.g., agranulocytosis) while underweighting the mortality risk from untreated severe mental illness, particularly suicide. The argument is plausible but relies on narrative reasoning rather than empirical data. No effect sizes or statistical comparisons are provided.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The piece suggests that clinicians may be overly cautious about clozapine due to historical fears, potentially denying patients a life-saving treatment. It does not change practice directly but may encourage a re-evaluation of risk-benefit assessments in clozapine prescribing.

item.title: Classroom-based observation and intervention of executive function for special education teachers working with preschoolers with Autism.
item.description: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Executive function (EF) related behavioral challenges are frequently observed in preschool children with autism spectrum disorder. However, structured, classroom-based observation of these behaviors by teachers remains difficult, resulting in limited practical assessment and recommendations for classroom-based support. This study aimed to examine the feasibility of teacher-administered EF assessment in special education centers and to formulate preliminary, expert-informed recommendations for autistic children with varying communication abilities.

item.title: Preliminary Evaluation of Implementation and Effectiveness of the Relational Suicide Intervention Pilot.
item.description: Although primary interventions for suicidal ideation typically focus on individuals, couple-based clinical interventions for this population remain underdeveloped. Despite emerging evidence suggesting that relational interventions may improve suicidal ideation, currently only one couple-based intervention has preliminary evidence, and it was specifically designed for military couples. This gap highlights the need for systemic couple-based interventions in outpatient settings.

item.title: Advancing the use of artificial intelligence in psychiatry: The need for international collaboration.
item.description: Challenging macrotrends in recent decades have characterised population mental health across the globe, with apparent deterioration in adolescent mental health, as well as underfunded, inequitable, and inefficient psychiatric care systems [1]. Unnecessary delays to treatment are widespread, with systemic difficulties, such as clinician burnout, a dearth of funding, and staff shortages, negatively impacting mental health care across Europe and beyond [2]. With limited clinician time and resources available, new methods for improving mental health care are an urgent priority.

item.title: Medical assistance in dying on psychiatric versus somatic grounds: survey on the experiences of relatives.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Relatives are often intimately involved in medical assistance in dying (MAID) on both psychiatric and somatic grounds. Greater insight into the extent to which certain experiences occur in practice will help physicians provide support. AIMS: To investigate how relatives of patients who received psychiatric versus somatic MAID scored on measures of opinions and emotions regarding the MAID trajectory; involvement in the trajectory; and judgement of the due care criteria.

item.title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function.
item.description: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets.

item.title: Characterizing gradients of functional connectome underpinning rumination and their alteration in depression.
item.description: As a prominent psychopathological process of major depressive disorder (MDD), rumination's brain underpinnings remain unclear. Emerging studies have highlighted that the brain is organized along several macroscale gradients, which could serve as a powerful framework for better understanding how the functional connectome underlies rumination. In this study, we leveraged two datasets (Rum-Beijing and Rum-MDD) to characterize the gradient structure during an active ruminative state.

item.title: The paradox of high IQ in ADHD: dissociable effects on inattention and impulsivity - insights from behavior, cognition & brain in 5138 children.
item.description: While Intelligence Quotient (IQ) is widely considered a linear protective factor against attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), this paradigm fails to capture domain-specific nuances. We investigated whether non-linear relationships between IQ profiles and ADHD symptoms exist in a large cohort of children diagnosed with ADHD using a multidimensional dataset that integrates behavioral assessments, cognitive testing, and neuroimaging data.

item.title: Post-Diagnosis Depression and Suicide Risk Among Cancer Survivors: A Nationwide Population-Based Cohort Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Patients with cancer are at increased risk of suicide, but the contribution of depression arising after cancer diagnosis remains poorly characterised. AIMS: To evaluate whether first-recorded depression after cancer diagnosis was associated with subsequent suicide risk among adults with cancer who had no documented depression before cancer diagnosis. METHODS: Using the South Korean National Health Insurance Service database. 755,079 adults newly diagnosed with cancer between 2009 and 2013, without documented depression before cancer diagnosis, were followed through 2023.

item.title: Acute Psychosis and Dissociative Syndrome Following Binge Recreational Nitrous Oxide Use: A Case Report.
item.description: Recreational nitrous oxide (N2O) inhalation is increasingly prevalent among young adults, but acute psychiatric presentations following short-term binge exposure remain poorly characterized. We report a case of a female in her early 20s with no prior history of psychotic illness who developed an acute psychotic and dissociative syndrome over three days at an outdoor music festival. Her presentation followed heavy recreational N2O and 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) exposure combined with sleep deprivation.

item.title: Prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among undergraduate health professions students in Borama, Somaliland: a cross-sectional study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Mental disorders are characterized by significant impairments in an individual's thoughts, emotional control, and patterns of behavior. University students frequently suffer from mental disorders like depression, anxiety, and stress. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among undergraduate health professions students in Borama, Somaliland. METHODS: An institution-based quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 315 undergraduate health professions students from October to December 2025.

item.title: Deviations from the standard of care in the treatment of pregnant people with opioid use disorder in jails; a mixed methods study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) with methadone or buprenorphine are the standard of care for opioid use disorder (OUD) during pregnancy and postpartum. MOUD is not routinely available in US jails. Little is known about OUD management practices and patient experiences when MOUD is unavailable in jails. This study aims to assess deviations from standard pregnancy OUD care in jail and demonstrate patients' experiences of such deviations.

item.title: Prescribing to protect case series: naltrexone as a novel intervention to prevent fentanyl overdose in people who use cocaine.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The rise in fentanyl contamination of cocaine has contributed to a surge in opioid-involved overdose deaths among people who use cocaine (PWUC). Existing harm reduction strategies, including naloxone distribution, drug checking, and counseling people to use with others, are inadequate in fully addressing this risk. Despite robust evidence supporting contingency management (CM) as an effective treatment for cocaine use disorder (CUD), its implementation remains limited.

item.title: Co-Designed Best Practice Principles for the Care of Fathers and Non-Birthing Parents Exposed to Perinatal Trauma: A Participatory Action Research Study.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: To co-design best practice principles (BPPs) for providing compassionate, holistic support to fathers and non-birthing parents exposed to perinatal trauma. DESIGN: Participatory action research methodology to generate qualitative data. SETTING, PARTICIPANTS: Face-to-face workshops were conducted across the Greater Brisbane area and online workshops were held for national consultation from 23 April 2024 to 27 May 2025. Fathers and non-birthing parents with lived experience of perinatal trauma and a multidisciplinary team of health and community care professionals were included.

item.title: Experiences of Self-Identified Antenatal Depressive Symptoms Among Expectant Fathers in Northeastern Thailand: A Qualitative Study.
item.description: Depression is a major global health concern, particularly during the transition to fatherhood. This study explored and described the experiences of self-identified antenatal depressive symptoms among expectant fathers. A qualitative design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with eighteen participants who screened positive for depressive symptoms on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Participants were recruited from antenatal clinics in eight public hospitals in a northeastern province of Thailand, and all had partners with 12 to 40 weeks of pregnancy.

item.title: Postoperative Risks in Thoracolumbar Fractures Patients with Mental Disorders: A Retrospective Cohort Study Using a Nationwide Inpatient Database.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Mental disorders, such as schizophrenia and mood disorders, are associated with spine injuries. However, the relationship between mental disorders and short-term outcomes after surgery for spine injury remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between mental disorders and postoperative outcomes in surgical patients with thoracolumbar fractures. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study was performed using a national inpatient database in Japan.

item.title: Childhood traumatic experiences and postpartum depression: a mixed methods narrative study.
item.description: PURPOSE: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a significant public health concern with profound effects on the health and well-being of women, children, and families. A growing body of research has identified an association between childhood traumatic experiences and an increased risk of PPD. This study aims to elucidate potentially underrecognized childhood experiences that are perceived as traumatic or particularly formative, and to examine whether linguistic features in brief trauma narratives are associated with PPD symptomatology.

item.title: Sex-dependent effects of imperatorin on autistic-like behaviors and BDNF signaling in rats prenatally exposed to valproic acid.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined by cognitive impairments such as learning and memory decline, and social interaction and communication deficits. This study investigated the potential effects of Imperatorin (IMP), a furocoumarin and a phytochemical isolated from the leaves of Ferulago trifida on valproic acid (VPA)-induced behavioral and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) alterations in a rat model of ASD.

item.title: Neurobehavioral Profiles and Clinical Consequences of MYT1L-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Insights From the Brain Gene Registry.
item.description: MYT1L-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (MYT1L-NDD) is a rare autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by intellectual disability, global developmental delay, autism, and obesity. Despite growing recognition, prospective and systematic clinical phenotyping remains limited. Here, we present an exploratory analysis of data from 25 individuals with MYT1L-NDD enrolled in the Brain Gene Registry (BGR), a national platform integrating genetic, neurobehavioral, and clinical data.

item.title: Mental health outcomes in Prader-Willi Syndrome: An Australian cohort study.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is an imprinting disorder associated with complex cognitive, physical, and behavioral features, as well as high rates of mental health conditions. Understanding mental health conditions in individuals with PWS and their association with behavioral characteristics is an essential step towards better supporting individuals with PWS.

item.title: Gaps in Support for Two Autistic Individuals in Adulthood: A Case Report.
item.description: The transition to adulthood can leave autistic people without the educational, therapeutic, social, and community supports available earlier in life. Adults identified as autistic later in life may encounter a different but related gap, receiving a meaningful explanation for longstanding experiences without obtaining the practical support needed to pursue education, employment, relationships, or community participation. This report describes two autistic individuals whose different trajectories converged in a shared loss of continuity.

item.title: Caregiver-implemented standardized-to-individualized behavior-analytic toilet-training package for preschoolers with autism.
item.description: Children with autism often face challenges with incontinence and may benefit from more structured toilet training relative to neurotypical children. In the current study, we evaluated a standardized-to-individualized behavior-analytic toilet-training package with caregivers as the interventionists. We used telehealth to train caregivers remotely to support their implementation of the procedures and obtain additional data on implementation and outcomes. Four preschool-aged children with autism and their caregivers participated.

item.title: Trends in Australian Alcohol Consumption and Related Harms, 2010-2023.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Alcohol consumption is a substantial contributor to Australia's total disease burden. Various studies have examined trends in specific measures of consumption or harm, but a comprehensive analysis of trends is needed to understand the changing impact of alcohol in Australia. The current study synthesised data across multiple national indicators to assess long-term trends in alcohol consumption and related harms.

item.title: Pharmacogenetic Impact of CYP2C19 Variants on Diazepam Treatment Outcomes in Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome.
item.description: Diazepam (DZP) is widely accepted as an effective pharmaceutical intervention for treating Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (AWS), and its efficacy and metabolic profile are influenced by genetic variations in the CYP2C19 gene. The objective of the present study was to investigate the impact of the CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*17 phenotypes on DZP metabolism. Whole blood samples were collected from 114 patients with AWS following a 10-day course of oral DZP therapy. Genotyping was performed using PCR-RFLP. Plasma concentrations of DZP and nordiazepam (NDZP) were determined using HPLC-UV.

item.title: [Opioid usage in Denmark].
item.description: The debate on an opioid crisis in Denmark points in two directions. While prescriptions for opioids are declining, there is a marked increase in illegal use, predominantly among young people. There is still a lack of knowledge in the healthcare system regarding optimal dosing, treatment duration, and the risk of dependence. In addition, evidence is limited on the sharing of leftover prescription medications between citizens and on systematic monitoring of illegal opioid use. This review concludes that a comprehensive national strategy is needed to prevent an opioid crisis in Denmark.

item.title: [Clinical challenges and toxicology of nitazenes].
item.description: Nitazenes are 2-benzylbenzimidazole opioids never approved for medical use. They are highly potent, up to 500-fold stronger than heroin, and overdoses may require higher naloxone doses compared with overdoses caused by other opioids. They are found on the illicit drug market, but their presence in Denmark - particularly in counterfeit tablets - appears to be limited. Fatal cases have occurred, and forensic detection is challenged by very low lethal concentrations. Collaboration between authorities, clinicians and forensic toxicologists is crucial to prevent nitazene-related deaths in Denmark.

item.title: Polygenic risk for schizophrenia predicting age-specific fluctuations in depressive symptoms: Findings from the Young Finns Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: A well-established connection exists between psychoses and depression, with one presentation being depressive symptoms before psychosis. However, the predictive power of preceding affective symptoms is reported to be low, raising the question whether depressive symptoms could reflect intermediary phenotypes associated with high polygenic risk for schizophrenia (PRSscz). We examined whether PRSscz is associated with depressive symptoms from adolescence to middle age in those who did not develop a non-affective psychosis.

item.title: Association of peripartum cardiomyopathy with psychiatric disorders - a narrative review.
item.description: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a myocardial disease characterized by a decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction below 45%, developing at the end of pregnancy or within a few months after its termination. It is a condition with multifactorial etiology that remains incompletely elucidated. Presumed pathophysiological mechanisms include excessive oxidative stress and abnormal prolactin and tryptophan metabolism. These mechanisms may also underlie the development of psychiatric disorders, which occur more frequently in patients with PPCM than in women without the condition.

item.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for the treatment of restless legs syndrome: A meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This meta-analysis examined whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) reduces symptoms in patients with Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) compared with sham stimulation, pooling data from four small controlled studies.
FINDINGS: Across four studies, rTMS significantly lowered IRLS-RS scores (MD 6.46, 95 % CI 4.44–8.48, P < .00001) and PSQI sleep scores (MD 4.80, 95 % CI 3.51–6.08, P < .00001). Subgroup analyses suggested benefit for both low- and high-frequency rTMS, but no effect on PSQI in primary RLS (MD 1.86, 95 % CI –2.65–6.37, P = .42) and no improvement in anxiety or depression scales.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by the small number of studies (n = 4), modest sample sizes, and heterogeneity in stimulation parameters and RLS subtypes. Effect sizes on IRLS-RS and PSQI are statistically significant but may not reach clinically meaningful thresholds for many patients. The lack of benefit on mood scales and the single negative PSQI subgroup raise concerns about robustness. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized protocols and longer follow-up are needed before rTMS can be recommended for routine RLS care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify adopting rTMS for RLS outside research settings; clinicians should await confirmatory trials before considering this intervention.

item.title: Ketamine in psychiatry: a systematic review of clinical applications, safety considerations, and emerging challenges.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on ketamine’s psychiatric applications, mechanisms, safety, and challenges, addressing its evolution from anesthesia to experimental treatments for psychiatric disorders. It aggregates findings across 106 peer-reviewed publications to evaluate clinical utility, risks, and research gaps.
FINDINGS: Ketamine acts primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist, triggering downstream effects such as increased glutamate transmission, AMPA receptor activation, BDNF expression, synaptogenesis, and mTOR pathway signaling. Clinically, it is used for anesthesia, treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and pain, with off-label interest in PTSD, anxiety disorders, and bipolar disorder. The review highlights challenges including recreational misuse, safety monitoring needs, and ethical considerations around telehealth prescribing of oral/sublingual formulations.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis without meta-analytic pooling, this review provides a broad overview but lacks quantitative effect sizes or direct comparisons between interventions. Strengths include integration across disciplines and identification of key gaps (e.g., long-term safety, optimal dosing, and patient selection). Limitations include heterogeneity of included studies and absence of formal risk-of-bias assessment. The clinical significance of findings remains uncertain due to the descriptive nature of the evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Ketamine may offer rapid but transient relief for TRD and certain pain conditions, but routine use requires careful risk-benefit assessment due to safety concerns and recreational risks. Clinicians should monitor for dissociative effects, abuse potential, and ensure structured follow-up—especially with novel formulations. Further high-quality trials are needed to define long-term efficacy and safety.

item.title: Excessive Yawning During Escitalopram Therapy in a Rwandan Woman with Co-Morbid Depression and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: A Case Report.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether excessive yawning can be an adverse effect of escitalopram in a patient with depression and PTSD. This case report from Rwanda describes a single patient’s experience to highlight a rare but recognized side effect of SSRIs.
FINDINGS: A 44-year-old Rwandan woman with severe depression and PTSD developed approximately six yawning episodes every 15 minutes three days after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily. The yawning was not attributed to other medical, neurological, or sleep-related causes, nor to concurrent short-term diazepam use. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 5, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction. The yawning decreased substantially by the two-week follow-up while escitalopram was continued.
INTERPRETATION: As a case report, this study provides very low-quality evidence limited to a single patient. The Naranjo score suggests a probable but not definitive causal relationship. The lack of a control group, small sample size (n=1), and short follow-up duration (two weeks) limit generalizability. The clinical significance of yawning as an adverse effect is uncertain, but awareness may prevent unnecessary investigations and treatment changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that excessive yawning can occur early in escitalopram treatment and may not warrant immediate discontinuation if the antidepressant benefit is emerging. However, this single case should not change practice without further evidence.

item.title: Amygdala neurofeedback as an adjunct to residential dialectical behavior therapy for borderline personality disorder: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by affective instability and amygdala hyperreactivity. Although dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) reduces symptoms and amygdala-related abnormalities, many patients show only partial remission. Real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) amygdala neurofeedback (amy-NF) directly targets hyperactive limbic responses and has shown promise in uncontrolled trials. We examined whether amy-NF adds benefit to inpatient DBT.

item.title: Exploring suicide among immigrant farmworkers in the United States: evidence from the National Violent Death Reporting System.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Agricultural workers face some of the highest suicide rates in the United States, yet limited research has examined suicide among immigrant and migrant farmworkers (IMFs), a population recognized as particularly vulnerable within occupational health surveillance priorities. This study examined circumstances contributing to suicide among IMFs and compared these to circumstances among U.S.-born farmworkers using National Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS) data.

item.title: Psychiatric morbidity is associated with cognitive impairment, whereas diagnostic category may shape its profile: a transdiagnostic study of inflammation, salivary biomarkers, and health-related quality of life.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Cognitive impairment is highly prevalent across psychiatric disorders, but it remains unclear how psychiatric morbidity and diagnostic category contribute to its presence and profile and whether inflammation and salivary synaptic proteins are associated with cognitive impairment across diagnoses. This transdiagnostic study integrated clinical, cognitive, inflammatory, and salivary biomarker data to examine these questions.

item.title: The active self in autism: multisensory and sensorimotor foundations of bodily self-representation.
item.description: The active self, understood as the embodied sense of self arising from goal-directed action and interaction with the environment, is supported by sensorimotor processes including multisensory integration and proprioception. Atypical self-representation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been proposed to relate to differences in these processes. To clarify this relationship, we conducted a systematic conceptual review of 37 empirical studies published between 2010 and August 2025 examining multisensory and bodily components of the active self in ASD.

item.title: The Importance of Translational Research for Neurodevelopmental Disorders and Autism Spectrum Disorders.
item.description: Translational research is the process of transforming fundamental biological discoveries into safe and efficacious interventions for patients. This specialized field is of particular importance for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), a broad class of behaviorally defined conditions including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDDs), and related disorders.

item.title: A Novel De Novo Heterozygous Missense Variant in CTNNB1 (c.2215A>C, p.Met739Leu) Underlying Neurodevelopmental Disorder With Spastic Diplegia and Visual Defects (NEDSDV): A Case Report.
item.description: We report a 7-year-old male with microcephaly, spasticity, strabismus, dysmorphism, autistic behaviors, and moderate ID due to a novel de novo likely pathogenic CTNNB1 variant (c.2215A>C, p.Met739Leu). This case underscores Whole Exome Sequencing's diagnostic utility for early detection of rare monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders.

item.title: Past, present, and future of non-pharmacological interventions for autism spectrum disorder: A global bibliometric and thematic analysis (2001-2025).
item.description: BACKGROUND: Non-pharmacological interventions (NPIs) have become increasingly important in addressing the complex and heterogeneous needs of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly in light of the limitations associated with pharmacological treatments. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to systematically map the global research landscape and thematic evolution of NPIs for ASD from 2001 to 2025 using bibliometric approaches. METHODS: A total of 341 English-language articles were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection.

item.title: Navigating professional oral care for autistic children: a qualitative study with parents.
item.description: PURPOSE: Despite growing recognition of inclusion health, autistic children continue to face inequities in accessing dental care. This qualitative study explored how a sample of parents in Hong Kong navigated professional oral care for their autistic children to better understand the perceived barriers and facilitators to dental visits and treatment, as well as strategies and adaptations that support successful dental care.

item.title: Sexual and gender identity differences in mental health concerns as a function of social media use and cyberbullying among U.S. youth.
item.description: As adolescents increasingly engage with social media, concerns have emerged about its potential implications for youth mental health and about disparities in digital experiences by sexual orientation (SO) and gender identity (GI). However, the mechanisms linking social media use (SMU) to mental health and SOGI disparities in digital contexts remain unclear.
